utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. May I remind you, your affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us continue where we left off yesterday. My next question pertains to the 26th of March. The time is 1600, 1630, in the village of Likovac. Do you know where the village of Likovac is?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also in the municipality of Srbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of this date, the 26th of March, and the time slot that I indicated? So do you know that in the village of Likovac five police officers were killed, or is it something that you don't know about?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In light of the fact that in your statement you said that you had received information from the KLA about all the events in the municipality of Srbica, how do you then explain the fact that you have no knowledge of such an extremely grave incident?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] In the place where I was operating, that was an area that was physically separated from Likovc that you mentioned. Likovc is south of Turiqevc, the terrain is very difficult, about 3 kilometres south of Turiqevc, so it is very difficult to communicate with people. Very often for days on end nobody came from Likovc to Turiqevc, and vice versa. I did not have any contact with people in Likovc. It would be impossible for me to get information about events in Likovc. They had other reporters who reported for the RTK and other media. So Likovc was not under my zone of responsibility, if I could call it so. I would comment on what you said, that it would not be reasonable to attack the Serb forces there. The Serb forces came to Izbica from various directions, and they did not have any connection with Likovc whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned your area of responsibility, and you have never done that before. Could you please then tell me, what was your area of responsibility in territorial terms, since you said that Likovac was not within your jurisdiction, that it was south of Turicevac about 3 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that I operated in the area of Brigade 111th. In Likovc there was another brigade; I can't remember its name or number. There were other people who were responsible there in Likovc. Brigade 112th was -- started from the area of Llausha, and I could mention all the villages under its responsibility, but it could take a long time. If you want me to do so, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to do that, but you claim that Likovac was not in your area, as you say it. Can we agree that it is a fact?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question again pertains to what you stated in your examination-in-chief when you were examined by my colleague, Ms. Daniela Kravetz. You said that on the 24th of March a shell killed three people in the village of Kladernica. Did you eye-witness that event?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not eye-witness that because I went there later. The event had occurred during the night, while I went there in the morning of the 25th of March. However, I did not have any reason that it happened, because I was in contact with people, with their relatives, so I got information from them. And this killing happened because of the shelling. The Serb forces here did not conduct any execution of the people, but people died because there was shelling. And these people, unfortunately, were there at the moment and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was shelling, that the village of Kladernica was shelled. You also mentioned that on the 26th, if I'm not mistaken, the 26th of March, a group of people was killed in Turicevac, again by shelling. Were you an eye-witness of this latter incident on the 26th? Rather, I'm sorry, yes, I made a mistake. It was the 30th of March. And the village is Tusilje. That was the other story about the shelling.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not eye-witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you heard this from other people. Those other people that you heard it from, were those officers of the KLA, in other words, the military, or were those civilians?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a group of people, villagers, who were in Tushile, and then they came to Kopiliq and I talked to them. They were scared, terrified, by what had happened that day and told me that in Tushile there had been a very severe shelling. I heard the shelling personally, but they told me that 11 people had been killed. I was never able to verify the information, though, so I'm not sure how many people died. But of course people died there. However, whether there were 11 of them or less, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, where did the shells come from, when we're talking about the village of Kladernica and the village of Tusilje?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to explain that the Serb forces, whenever we wanted to enter a place, first of all, they shelled is. That's why I always call them "the Serb forces" and not with another name, because my impression is that the Serb army shelled, and then after that the operations were joint operations, the police and the army. So if they had planned to enter a certain area, they shelled the whole day to show people where they were, and the people had to leave in order to be safe. They also wanted to show the KLA: Either fight us or leave. And I think that that was the reason. And they did not care where that shell fell and who it killed. They were not known for their humanitarian feelings. So at that time we knew where the Serb forces were because of the shelling and the source of the shelling. The source of the shelling for Klodernice and the other villages, because to go to Klodernice you have to go to Kastriot, they shelled all the villages around. They entered Klodernice, they entered Turiqevc, they rested in Turiqevc for a night, they shelled other villages. They did not go to Tushile the next day, but they waited so that they could enter Tushile after the shelling. And they did not want to have many losses on their side. This is how they operated. They went wherever they wanted and they had minimal losses on their part. It was a very well-organised army. The forces were well organised. Their operations were successful, but they harmed the local population, the civil population a lot, while the KLA did not resist, because that was their order from their commanders. And the civilian population asked them not to resist because they would not be able to push them back. So the result of the shelling was that the people would leave, go to places that they thought were safer, such as Izbica, and at the same time the KLA preserved its people. The idea was not to have many losses. The KLA avoided the conflict, while the Serb army shelled the villages without taking into account whether there were people there or not, and they didn't care whether they killed people or not. So the next day they would be able to enter the area. At that time the Serb operations were going on, the KLA were in the mountains around, and it is very interesting because the Serb forces never went to the mountains to look for the KLA. They didn't need to. This was their tactics. They wanted to kill the civilian population and not have any losses on their side. I think they achieved this successfully. But, however, the population was really harmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, you were in Lecina. Can you please repeat for us, why did you leave that place?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Leqina at the beginning, after my house was burnt. I lived in Demush Dragaj's house. The reason I left on the 26th is because it was impossible to go on living there. I went to Izbica, to Turiqevc, and at that time I could see what was going on. We measured the danger we were in by the shelling that was happening. So the shelling started on Leqina so I did not -- I could not go to Leqina anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to speak more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that the Serbian forces shelled Lecina, too.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces shelled all the villages in Dr enice, including Leqina. There is no village in Drenice that was not shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, were there any Serb inhabitants in those villages? That's my first question. And my second question is whether there were any other ethnic communities, non-Albanians, living there, members of other ethnic communities living in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my village, Padalishte, there were no Serbs. In Leqina there were some Serb families. In other villages, in Drenice, Ludoviq, Llausha, there is a church which was working before and during the war. In Runik where I worked as a doctor, there were Serbs. Runik had a majority of Serbs in the area. Then Banja and the village of Radisheva, there were Serbs. On the other side there is the village of Belinca, which is in the Istog municipality but is neighbouring to Izbica. That is another village where Serbs lived. This is what I know about what you asked me. In Leqina there were several families. Not many, but there were some. I did not have any contact with these Serbs personally, unless they came to Runik as patients for me to treat them. That could be possible. But other than that, I did not have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that a number of Serb families -- well, let's have Lecina as our example, because this is where you were; that there were at least ten Serb families there. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that you have the right information, but I don't know. I can agree with you, but I cannot say whether there were ten of them or how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you this because you spent some time there and you are familiar with the circumstances, and this is why I'm quite surprised that you're not aware of this. But I'm sure that there will be many things that you don't know when we come to things that you don't want to be talking about. But what I'm asking you now is this: The families living in Lecina, was their last name Smigic or Zmigic? Do you know at least that?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the surnames. I'm not sure. I will say again that it is possible that there were families with that surname, but I didn't know them. Well, as to your comment, I don't think that I have given the impression that I don't want to answer the questions; however, that's your opinion, and you can think whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to be mistaken. Of course, I simply presented my impression and it is not binding on anyone in this courtroom, but I'm sure that we will all be thinking about what you told us. My next question is, since you were in Lecina, and bearing in mind the way that you answered -- the way you answered questions so far, I think I have a fair idea of what your answer will be, but can you tell me, do you know who Habit Haziraj is, who Muhamet Haliti, aka Naser, who these people are? We're talking about Lecina. You lived there.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhamet Haliti, I don't think there is -- there was a Muhamet Haliti there. And this person Naser, who was that person?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I asked you. Do you know who he is, Muhamet Haliti, aka Naser?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no person with such a name in Leqina. I don't remember any Muhamet Haliti. In Leqina there are these names: Dragaj, Shala, Konjuhi, Haziraj, who live in another neighbourhood. There is another surname which is Shala. There are the Haziraj's and there are some other surnames, but there is no Haliti as a surname. I know the Albanians much better. Maybe it's another name you're thinking about. I have no reason to say I don't know him. I don't think, though, that there is a person with that surname in the village of Leqina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Loshi, I will agree with you completely for the last names that you mentioned, although I really don't know the families that you mentioned. I asked you about a name, whether you knew that man, but that pertained to Lecina. I asked you about Habit Haziraj. Can I elicit any kind of answer from you about that name? I don't claim that they are from Lecina, but they were linked to an event in Lecina that involved the Serb population. So that's why I'm asking you, do you know who Habit Haziraj is, yes or not, and if yes, then please explain how you know him.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Habit Haziraj was a member of the KLA. He was a member of the 112th Brigade. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where is Habit Haziraj from?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Llausha.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Lecina. My next question is this: Do you know that those two persons I just mentioned to you, Habit Haziraj and Muhamet Haliti, aka Naser, or since you told us that you didn't know who Muhamet Haliti was, do you have any knowledge of any persons having abducted Dostana Smigic form Lecina and having taken her to a prison in the village of Likovac. And she was killed after that. She was also tortured, and she went through a number of unpleasant experiences. Do you have any knowledge of that, since at that time you were in Lecina? Or, again, you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please give me a date because I have heard about this case, but I was not in Leqina at that time. I heard about this case when I was in Runik working there, meaning that a Serb woman was missing for some time. I was not in Leqina at the time so I don't have direct information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it probably happened before you arrived in Lecina. That's what I suppose.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I heard about that when I was in Runik, from the Albanians, Serbs, that this woman went missing, but I don't have any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What time -- when did you arrive in Lecina? What month?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Leqina by the end of June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there more Serbs in Lecina at that time? Were those families living there still, or had they already moved out?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that there were Serbs there, that their houses were there; however, please believe me that I don't know whether they were still living there or not. I was busy doing my job as a doctor. Their houses are in a separate neighbourhood. They have a different entrance from the rest of the village. You enter that neighbourhood through another street, so I never went to that neighbourhood. I simply don't have any information about what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us that those Serbs were hale and hearty to such an extent that they never went to visit Dr. Loshi, or was there any other doctor there or near?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when I worked in Leqina, you mean? They didn't come to see me. I don't know whether they had health problems or not, but they never came to see me as a doctor. If you ask me about Runik, then, yes, there were Serbs. Maybe there were some who came from Leqina, but I don't remember all of them. I had many patients, between 70 and 80 a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about Lecina, not Runik, and that was not by chance. There were the Serb houses there, the ones that you saw, but there were no Serbs living there. They had been expelled, as you saw. I'm going to stop at this point and then I'm going to deal with another topic. In relation to Tusilje and Kladernica, and we heard about other villages, you said that they were shelled by Serb forces and you said that was their pattern of behaviour. And they would enter and then they did all sorts of things, committed crimes, and so on and so forth. So we heard that there were Serbs in those villages, too, and we will conclude that the Serb army and police were merciless, as you say, towards the members of their own ethnic group that they belonged to. I would be interested in the shelling. First of all, when did the NATO bombing in Kosovo start? Do you know the date?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. Do you know and are you sure that the shelling that you referred to was carried out by the Serb army only, or was there shelling by NATO, too?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Drenice area, at least in the area where I lived, there was no shelling by NATO. In other words, there was no bombing by NATO from the air. The shelling came from the Serb forces, land forces, from their positions on the ground, so they were shelling surface to surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, where did you do your military service? You said that you had done your military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, so where was that?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to do military service in September 1987 and completed it in 1988. I completed one part in Bitola, in Macedonia, and I finished the training period there in Bitola, or Manastir in Albanian, and the remaining part I completed in Skopje. The training period lasted for some three months.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly requests that the witness repeats the dates again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] September 1987, and September 1988 I finished it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for such a detailed answer. Just one more detail, please. What service did you do your military service in, and what were you trained for?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taught how to use automatic rifles, pistols, recoilless guns. To tell you the truth, I was not a weapon lover, so it is very difficult for me to remember every type of weapons we were taught how to use. I don't like weapons. I was not a good soldier in terms of weapons, using weapons. I was 27 when I went to do my military service and completed it when I was 28, so my interests were completely different. So going to serve, to do the military service, for me was like going to prison. But that was something that we all had to do, so that's what I did, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I share your views on a personal level. Just one more thing. As you described this to all of us in the courtroom, did you serve in the infantry or where? I'm talking about arms and services now. It certainly wasn't the navy. I doubt it was the air force.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- we underwent the general training. I was in the infantry for three and a half months, until this training period was completed, and afterwards I was no longer part of the infantry. We worked in the Goca Delcev barracks and did physical work, manual work. And I also had time to prepare my exams, so at the same time I was studying to complete my university studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And you were not a good soldier; right?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to using weapons, yes, I was not a good soldier. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, yes, yes. Since you mentioned your young colleague who worked as a doctor together with you and who got killed later, you said that he got his degree in medicine from a university that was not recognised by the Serbian authorities, so he did not have a diploma, whereas you graduated from the school of medicine from the University of Pristina within the educational system of the then SFRY or later FRY, and within that, of course, the Republic of Serbia, the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija. Am I right when I say that? And you got a regular diploma of the school of medicine of the University of Pristina; right?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague, too, had a diploma, but from an alternative university led by Albanians. So he graduated from this faculty. He had a diploma too. Personally, I graduated as you explained during the time of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What KLA brigade operated in the area of Izbica or, rather, Srbica, one or more? And if so, which one or which ones?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One so-called brigade, though it wasn't a brigade in real terms. I don't know about the exact number of soldiers. I was asked of this from Milosevic, during that trial. This was a brigade that operated in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This so-called brigade, as you had put it, was that the Drenica operation zone of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this brigade, during 1998, and in the beginning of 1999 was in the Drenica operation zone or, rather, the municipality of Srbica; that they blocked roads there, attacked the Serb police, civilians, other ethnic groups, Roma included, and even Albanians who did not support their cause. Of course they attacked the security forces, the Serbian army, and so on. The question was a pretty long one, but the answer can be short.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not true. This brigade, like all other brigades that were formed, its purpose was to defend the Albanian population to a certain extent from the Serbian forces. We all knew that the brigade could not stop the attacks of the Serb forces when they were on offensive. If a group of Serbian infantry would enter a village, the idea was that these brigades, with a scarce number of weapons that they had, would defend the population and themselves. I'm not familiar with what you said, that they blocked the roads and killed civilians and that they killed Serbs and Albanians, civilians I mean. I know that they did kill policemen where they could. And if they confronted other police forces, there were probably casualties. But as far as civilians are concerned, Albanians, Roma, and other ethnic groups, I don't think so, at least I don't have any knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This does not correspond to part of your statement where it says that you were a doctor in Runik and that you know that a woman was abducted and went missing from the village of Lecina, but let it be. And there weren't any check-points on the roads, and the roads weren't blocked?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an answer. When I heard about this woman that had been abducted -- you're asking me about the activities of the 112th Brigade. At that time this brigade did not exist, at the time when this woman was abducted. There was one general name, KLA, and at that time I had no knowledge about the activities. It's a question of time. You're saying 1998, late 1998, beginning of 1999. Then, yes, there was a brigade. But if you're talking about the time of Runik, and you're linking that time to this brigade, I'm simply telling you that at that time the brigade didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And the brigade was established only to protect Albanian civilians, and it didn't have any other objectives; right? Are you trying to say that the sole objective of all the members of the KLA was not to the Republic of Kosovo, an independent Kosovo, an independent state of Kosovo, or was their objective only what you referred to, the defence of Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that their objective was to come out of a regime of that time, Milosevic time. I don't want to speak about this because we've heard a lot about this. But it was a difficult regime for the Albanians living in Kosova, so it had to come to an end by all means. We had Rugova as a leader who led for ten years the peaceful resistance, but then we realised that we could no longer understand each other with Milosevic through dialogue. So the idea was to free Kosova and afterwards to make Kosova independent. This is true, but the capabilities of the KLA to achieve such a thing was almost inexistent. As to the capabilities of the KLA to try and defend the population, this was possible, and that's why I'm saying that this was the tactics of the KLA. Maybe during the war they thought that they will liberate Kosova, that they're able to do this and that, but the reality was completely difficult. It didn't turn out as they expected, so their tactics was to defend the population to the extent that they could. As I mentioned earlier, the Serb army was very well organised. It was a strong army and used all its resources to meet its objectives. To what I saw, the objective was killing, inflicting horror and terror among the population, as well as fear, and ultimately force the Albanian population in Kosova to leave towards Albania and Macedonia, as we saw. This is what you've probably seen as well, something that the whole world has seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Obviously you will not agree with me that the Serb army and police in Kosovo and Metohija protected the sovereignty of a sovereign state, in view of mass armed resistance, attacks against Serb civilians, Serb police, and the Serb army. You certainly will not agree with me when I say that.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot defend sovereignty by mass killings, and this is what the Serb army and police did in fact. If they thought that they could defend sovereignty of their state, Serbian state, in this way, then I think that they were mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As you said, a discussion on that topic would be a very wide-ranging one, and we are not here for that purpose. However, you will agree with me that peoples like Albanians and people of the Falkland islands, who are tens of thousands of miles away from Great Britain, you know how they reacted when Argentina tried to annex that territory. Are we going to talk about the Basque in Spain? Do they have the same rights as Albanians? Not to speak about the recently seceded republics in Georgia. This is a political issue and one we are not dealing with in this courtroom, but we are now dealing with the consequence of a highly uncivilised, uncultured event, something that is wrong in the twentieth and twenty-first century, and I'm going to end on that note. What I'd like to say --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my colleague is again entering into a debate with the witness, and he's not putting any questions to him and entering into a debate with the witness. I'm just looking at the last line of the transcript. I don't see any question being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend Ms. Kravetz rightly noted that I went beyond the scope of questions being put to the witness, and I will agree with that. All of this provides an indispensable context for the questions that will follow, a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, my next question: You said that many people had come to Izbica; 20.000 to 25.000, that was your estimate. You said that they came from different villages, from the territory of Drenica. Why was it Izbica in particular that they came to?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned early, Izbica is a location where they sheltered. It's a valley with hills on both sides, and it suited the people at the time because they didn't want to be victims of shelling. So that's why they thought that they would be safe there. There's no other reason than that. The same situation is in Tushile. The terrain is more or less similar to that in Izbica; valleys, surrounded by hills. The Serb forces loved the hills. They wanted to be on top of the hills, and as soon as they entered the valleys, they would have already surrounded, encircled, them and they had free hands to do whatever they pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who is Zeqir Loshi. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a fellow villager, a distant relative of mine. There are three Loshi neighbourhoods there. He's not in my neighbourhood; he is from another neighbourhood. But he's not part of my family. We are very, very distant relatives, but I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Xhavit Dragaj is and Ramadan [Realtime transcript read in error "Ramut"] Dragaj?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have "Ramut Dragaj" on the screen before me. It should read Ramadan Dragaj. Xhavit Dragaj is a friend of mine. He's a doctor. We worked together. He's a dentist, and as I said, we worked together in Runik. Ramadan Dragaj, I didn't remember him as a name in the beginning, but later I was asked about him. Personally, I don't know him. But when I went to make a recording after the war about a massacre at Padalishte, he has allegedly come there, and allegedly I have presented him as Commander Ramadan. So this is how I came to realise that I've known -- I've met this person. I'm not describing him in any capacity. To me he was just a villager. It is possible that he was a KLA member, an ordinary soldier, but I don't think I heard of him having an important function within the KLA, whereas Xhavit was never a KLA member. He is a good doctor, a good dentist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your relative Zeqir?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeqir was for some time in Germany. He came back. I think I met him when I came back from Albania. I don't really remember. The Tribunal must have this footage about the massacre at Padalishte. This person was a civilian; I know him as such. I'm not sure whether he joined the KLA later or not. It is possible that he joined, but this I don't know. I cannot be specific here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm going to skip my next question. You mentioned what you term as the massacre in Izbica. You mentioned your relatives Sami and Jashar Loshi who lost their lives there. Can you tell me about the two of them? Were they members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they never were KLA members. This is -- they come from a very good family, very honest and helpful. So they were down-to-earth people, very good men, and they were never KLA members. They were close relatives and my first neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So they're from Padaliste; right?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are from Padalishte. Selman lived in Padalishte during this time, while Jashar and his son Sami lived in Skenderaj. So Jashar had his family in Skenderaj; however, during the war they joined together on the 20th, when 16 civilians were killed, the event that was mentioned and that occurred in Skenderaj. So these were amongst those who fled, who survived the events. They fled to Izbica, and they were killed there. I saw him with my own eyes -- I saw them with my own eyes, and I spoke to them about these events. I saw them on the night of the 27th of March for the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question has to do with Izbica. You arrived at the scene where you made the recording that we saw in the courtroom on the 30th of March. Now, my question pertains to all those people that you filmed, primarily to what you said. You said that you knew that some of them had not been killed on the same day as the majority of the civilians there. Of course, you were not an eye-witness; you learned that from conversations with other people. So now I'm going to ask you this: Do you know how many people that you filmed there were really residents of certain villages from the area around Izbica? Because it's quite obvious that people gathered there from various villages. And how many of them were killed in other locations? Is it just the one man that you mentioned or were there several?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I get the list here, I could help you. I can look at the surnames and then tell you which villages they come from. For example, there are people with the surname Dragaj; they are from Leqina and Izbica. Well, your question was how many people were from Izbica and the surrounding areas. That was the question I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. It is quite clear that all those people were from the area of Srbica, Drenica, and so on. What I'm asking you is, do you know for a fact whether all of them were killed, lost their lives, on that day, whatever, the 26th or 27th of March? Or were there people who were killed earlier or later?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, then. The two soldiers from the KLA are Zaim Bajrami and Ajet Beqiri. Ajet was wearing uniform; Zaim was in civilian clothes. They were killed at the same place on the 27th of March. The other people were killed on the 28th of March, all of them killed on the 28th of March. In the group of 127 people that I am talking about, they were all killed on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loshi. The next line of questioning will have to do with an exhibit tendered by the Prosecution. It's the list about the photograph where you answered some questions by my colleague Ms. Kravetz, and there was the investigator Malvin Dagsland, pertaining to the number of photographs that he did by getting screen caps from the footage and giving them numbers and providing some comments, in the statement as it has been written, and that has to do with the 23rd and the 25th of September, 2001. You said on that occasion that the film was done by Mr. Sefedin Thaqi, the teacher. You believe that he is still in Kosovo and that he's still in the same line of business. As regards the table, you testified in the Milutinovic et al case, and when Judge Bonomy --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to ask, if possible, to show the witness a portion of the transcript. That's page 50 -- 5401 of the transcript from the Milutinovic et al case, and if we could zoom on that page, 5401, paragraphs 5, 7, 8, and 9, those lines, rather, in the transcript. I would just like to say that this is D001-3962. In fact, 3862. [In English] It's page 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I do have information about this, I would just like to ask Dr. Loshi if he reads and understands English well.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The last time I witnessed I spoke in English, so I can recognise my words. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. We have to do this because this is a new and separate case. My question about this page is -- well, you told Judge Bonomy that you recognised all the words, that there is a comment by the investigator and that not all of those comments were given by him and not all the information was given by him or you, and especially not the words that are contained in the columns. That's what you said. And you go on to explain that it's possible that the investigator himself provided those descriptions, you see that, and that he obtained them from another witness, not from you. And you told us yesterday - that's in the transcript - that you provided the comments that are contained in the columns but that you can't remember now because a long time had passed. You talked about the first name mentioned in the column, but because of the time lapse you cannot recall. So how come there is this discrepancy between what you said yesterday and what you said at that time?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no discrepancy. It's only the way I said things. Before I did not have the list before me when I explained it. I am not an investigator, and I don't know how they work. When I came here and did the proofing, I asked the Prosecutor to give me again the contested part to see, the part that was discussed the last time I was here when I witnessed. And I was clear about what I said. I say that there were only two soldiers of the KLA, while here it appears as if there were an additional two. The truth is that there were only two soldiers of whom one was wearing uniform and the other was in civilian clothes. Well, with regard to the columns, the description of the bodies was done by the investigator himself in most of the cases, and I think that's normal because we viewed the tape together. I helped him with the identification and other things, but, however, the way people looked in the photographs, on the monitor, he described them. I agreed with his description and signed everything. So I don't think you can contest this. There was a confusion the last time, in the last trial, and now I can explain it in detail, if you want, if you wish. It was suggested that two people, one of them had a military jacket on or a military coat, [in English] which in fact the military court, military jacket, not necessarily presents the KLA soldier or any soldier at all. So I was confused that if somebody is suggesting me that what has been said about these two people as members of KLA, that was not true. They were not members of KLA. And I -- I wished if Prosecutor or yourself, if you have those pictures, to show them to the Judge and to show to me and so everyone can see them, that they don't look like soldiers. They're just like civilians. [Interpretation] I'll continue in Albanian. This is just because of the digression I had to make. I wanted to explain that concrete situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But what stuck in my memory and what I wanted to ask you about, why I wanted to get a brief and precise answer -- well, I got it, but it was not specific enough. It pertains to your argument. What you told us that all the comments in the columns where the people of their identities are described, that this is something that you did. And here you say something that is completely different, and this is why I had to ask you this. Now I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't have any other questions on this, but I would like to ask the usher: The page is 5402 -- no, 5403, so right after this document, and that would be page 51. Could we please look at that, and I would like to show this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is this: You state here that the only thing that you had to do with the table is that you were asked to sign it, you had a look at it, and then you signed it. We can look at the broader context of your statement. It particularly pertains to the person called Ajet Beqiri. That's paragraphs 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18. That's where it ends. So you simply state here that you signed the record and that this was all done by an investigator, and that you knew very little about it. You actually knew nothing about it. You stated something differently yesterday, so please could you just briefly comment on it.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I testified, I did not look into the details of the columns, and a long time had elapsed from 2001 when he came to Canada to 2006, five years had elapsed, and I dealt with other things in my life. So later on, when I looked at these lists more carefully, last week I mean, I saw that the comments are mine but the descriptions are the investigator's descriptions, where the people have been described, how they were dressed and so on. I, of course, accept this as my testimony and as my statement, but the last time I was confused. [In English] If somebody is suggesting me that there were two more soldiers in addition to two others I just mentioned, Ajet Beqiri and Zaim Bajrami, that is not true. So if somebody else wants to put two names here, then it's not -- it's not something that has to do with my testimony at all. But later on I figured out that it just -- it's a matter of misunderstanding. So the description has been done by the investigator of The Hague Tribunal, while the comments have been done by myself. And I take this as my testimony, and I signed it. There is nothing to dispute here, as far as myself is concerned at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is completely unclear to me, so I'm asking you why is it that you state this for the first time ten years after all this happened? Well, okay, 2001. Not ten but eight years. Why did you not say that when you testified in the Milutinovic case? Why did you describe things in a completely different way, saying that you did not know anything about the document more or less? And now you say that all the comments are yours. Is it possible that eight years after the events your memory is so much fresher, and it was not better two years before? So that's not logical at all.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If my memory had been as fresh now as it was eight years ago, yes, that would not be logical. But I will explain. The first time that I looked at this list in detail as a witness -- because before I came here as a witness, but I didn't think that I had to look at everything in detail. However, you, as Defence, are asking me questions, and from the previous experiences I thought that it would be better for me to look at everything I had said and signed. Well, in the Milosevic trial, the Prosecutor suggested that my witness statement included something by chance, something else; however, this had nothing to do with what the Prosecutor suggested. It had nothing to do with my testimony. It just had to do with something I failed to analyse before I came here. You can see for yourself here [in English] and see in 2002 what The Hague Prosecutor said about this case, and see that he was -- he was saying that there has been something else added to his testimony by chance, like not intentionally, and stuff like that. And that's why I was confused. So I thought when this question was put to me, then I thought, oh, probably this is something that belonged to that part that the Prosecutor was suggesting years ago in Milosevic trial. This is my answer about this, and I believe it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Loshi, I will not take your word for it that it makes sense. Logical errors that reveal the truth occur often in testimony, and this is what happened to you. You said, "I analysed the list this time." Why would you need to analyse it when you, yourself, provided the comments, when you took part in it, when you know all of it? You will remember that at any time if you did that, and you didn't, because if you had then the tone and the spirit of your testimony in the Milutinovic case would have been so different from what you're testifying to today. You will agree with me that you analysed it this time, and you were not called here to analyse it but to testify. Thank you. If you have a comment, I will gladly hear it.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did give my explanation, and you made a comment on it. You can comment however you like. My duty here is to present the facts and the Judges will analyse them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, my next question has to do with the bodies that you filmed there. Do you know for a fact that all the bodies were found -- that were found there, that they were really found there, that their lives ended there, or were there bodies that had been brought in from other places?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of the bodies were found in the two big groups and there was another smaller group, so in total three groups. I never counted the bodies myself, I think I mentioned that before; however, I gave a number, an approximate number, from 110 to 120 people that were killed. There were people who escaped, people who had wounds which were very heavy wounds, but they were able to move a little further until they died in another place, and they were found where they died. There were people who were brought from Izbica, again, but they were killed a little further; for example, somebody was killed in the mountain or in a meadow. However, all of them were killed in Izbica. For example, when the tape starts, you asked me, Why are you saying this is not your part? The person who is seen there lying down dead, this is a person who was killed by the Serb forces in Sefedin Thaqi's house, and his house was burnt by the Serb forces. His body was brought to Izbica because it's very close. It's about 500 or 600 metres away. So it was logical that all the people who were killed on that day, to be brought and buried there. So this is the body that is seen in -- on the tape. However, I say that this is not part of the Izbica massacre there. This person, however, was buried there, in Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that because of the flow of time, to have a break. But before that I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to admit into evidence the two pages that I quoted from, the pages in the Milutinovic et al case, the transcript in that case, page 5401 and page 5403. I've already provided the D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The second page was 5403, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had it as 5402.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Let me check. It won't take long, but I do believe it's 5403.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've been told that it was 3. You are correct, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those two pages will be received as the one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00024, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to continue my cross-examination after the break. It won't take long. But now I think it's a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, we are going back to the month of June when, in 1999, you returned to Tirana and when, according to your statement, you met up with a representative of an American organisation called the WITNESS, and you said that you got a camera from them. Could you please explain the details to us in reference to your contacts with this organisation? What do you know about this organisation? How did you get in touch with them, and what were the reasons that led them to give you this camera? What else did they give you, if anything, and what kind of contacts did you have with them afterwards? The question is a rather wide-ranging one, but it does merit an answer, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an organisation, though I've forgotten the details and information about it now. I think it's a humanitarian organisation called WITNESS. It's seat is in the US, in New York, as far as I recall. The meeting with them was initiated by them. At the time we met the bombing was still ongoing in Kosova, and from what they had seen from the media about the massacre at Izbica, they were quite enthusiastic to meet me. And they wanted to find other people as well who were interested to enter Kosova and film similar massacres or other things that were going on during the war there and afterwards provide this organisation with a recording. There was an agreement for these people to be paid afterwards. I don't remember the amount they were supposed to receive. And I don't know whether this agreement was realised in the end, because the bombing was still going on. The Serb forces, military and police, were not giving up, so it was impossible for me to enter Kosova. In the meantime they provided two or three colleagues of mine with cameras, too, because they, themselves, did not want to take the risk of going in, because during the bombing campaign in Kosova, the Serbian authorities did not allow a single foreign media to follow the developments there. Their interest was simply to get information. I think it was an organisation for protecting human rights, so that's why they provided us with cameras and tapes. So when I went eventually to Kosova, I took this opportunity to make some filming. I sent them the tape with the massacre at Padalishte, what I mentioned earlier, and I didn't give them any other material because that was of no interest to them. Then the war ended and this organisation was on its own then. So these were recordings from Kosova during the NATO campaign. I promised to enter Kosova, and I attempted to enter Kosova, but this was impossible without placing my life in danger. It was dangerous for everyone who tried to enter Kosova from Albania at that time. So I didn't go into Kosova, but I did after the bombing on the 20th of June, and on the 23rd I made the recordings that we saw yesterday here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loshi. Can you tell us the name of the person from this organisation called WITNESS that you got in touch with? And could you tell us when you were given this camera, what kind of a camera it was, and whether you took upon yourself some kind of obligation in respect to the technical equipment that you received from this person.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person was a female. I don't remember her name. She was a representative of this organisation based in Tirana at the time. We spoke, exchanged information. We received instructions from her for our work. She laid out the conditions to us and the obligation of the organisation towards us. The camera was the type with a tape. I think at the time there still were not -- there were no cameras of nowadays available. This was a camera with the smallest size of tapes, a Sony make, a hand-held camera, Sony make. I have the camera with me here, and I can offer the Tribunal to see it, to view it, if they so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, and I didn't ask you about this, under what circumstances were you working and what kind of instructions did you receive from this woman?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions were the following: We were supposed to record wherever possible, record massacres, what I did at Izbica, and provide them with the recordings. And they were supposed to pay us for every recording that we were going to make. I don't know the amount, whether it was 1.000 dollars or 2.000 dollars. I think it was 2.000 dollars per tape. Actually, not per tape but per incident. But we didn't manage to fulfil this agreement. We didn't receive any payment. I did take the camera, and I did send them the recordings of the Padalishte incident, and then we agreed that I keep the camera as a compensation for the recording, for the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May I conclude that you sent that organisation your footage from Padaliste as well?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I sent them a copy. I sent her a copy. I transferred the recording to another tape, and I sent them a copy. The original is with me. This happened after the war, and this is just to justify that they gave me the camera as a compensation for sending them this tape. However, the tape that I brought here with me, here I didn't provide anyone with that tape, only the Tribunal, the one that we saw yesterday. I sent them the copy by post, by mail, from Canada. I believe they have it. I didn't receive any confirmation from them, and I didn't have any further contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I wanted to ask you. Why did you not submit copies of the footage we saw yesterday to this organisation called WITNESS? As far as I understood things, in order to receive any money you had to have a certificate to the effect that you had carried out the duty that you had agreed upon with the representative of that organisation. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The massacre at Padalishte, I managed to record the decomposed bodies of the victims. When I went there, the bodies were still lying down there. So this was of greater interest to the representatives of this organisation, whereas the recordings at Izbica didn't show anything else but ground that used to be a gravesite but that was leveled afterwards. So they didn't take interest into this. I even thought that the tape would not be interesting for the Tribunal either. During my testimony here at the Milosevic -- Milutinovic trial, I did mention the fact that I do have the recordings that I made in Izbica in June 1999 upon my return from Albania, and then the Judge asked the Prosecution if they had this tape at their disposal. They said they didn't. And then I intervened by saying that I was never asked to provide the Prosecution with this tape and that I was ready to do that. So then the Prosecution asked me to give them the tape, and that's what I did. I believe I explained in general the idea why this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you do that, nevertheless, for the first time in the Milutinovic trial, seven years after you took the footage?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a matter of a context of a conversation. As a witness here, now, you're asking me questions; I'm answering your questions. So you might have noticed that I've provided you with more information, maybe things that I didn't mention in the past. Depending on the questions, on the context of the discussion, an event can be described from different angles by the same person, and now you're given an opportunity to look at the truth from all its angles, because I've come here to testify for three times here. However, the truth never changes; it always remains the same. What happened has happened, and that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you like to answer my question. Why did you do that only after seven years? For the first time it was in the Milutinovic case. That was when you mentioned the cassette for the very first time.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't think of it as an important document. I don't consider it an important documentation even now. This is a recording of the terrain in Izbica after the ground was leveled by the Serb forces and a recording that I made after the NATO forces entered Kosova on the 23rd of June, 1999. During that time, I saw some tables there and I realised from the people I spoke to there that there had been people from different international organisations. I even think that people from the Tribunal had been there before me. So I didn't see it as an important thing to mention. The trial admitted it as a document, received it as a document, as a proof that I was the person who did the recording and that this recording was made in 1999. So I don't know what other things to add. The footage depicts some gloves, some wood planks, some other items. You can tell that there had been bodies on that location; however, there are no other evidence -- there's no other evidence that may be of further use. I have no other comment to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to tell us the following: I viewed this footage very carefully. We can see you speaking in Albanian, in all fairness. Who actually held the camera in his or her hands and actually filmed this, while you were speaking?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I am speaking, that's the beginning of the recording, I've mentioned it earlier that the person who is holding the camera is Demush Dragaj, my friend. I went there with him. When I went to Kosova from Albania, I didn't have a car. I went to his house in Leqina and asked him to take me by car to the location in Izbica. So I gave him the camera, asked him to record me in front of the gravesite so that it is clearly seen who is making the report, and he's holding the camera. But when you don't see my face on the camera, during that time, it's me who is holding the camera. And you can hear my voice. You can tell from the voice that it is very close to the camera, while the other voice is a little bit more distant, and it's Demush's voice. He doesn't speak a lot on the tape, but I think you can hear his voice on several occasions. So when I asked him, for example, What is this? What is that? That voice is mine, and I'm the person holding the camera at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question -- there are only going to be two more questions, and that is going to conclude my cross-examination. So my first question has to do with the authenticity of the footage in relation to the date when it was made. Is there some compelling evidence that would prove the date when this was taken? Was it exactly June 1999? And my second question: As regards the film that had the working title "The Massacre in Izbica" - this concludes my cross-examination now - all the scenes the alleged massacre in Izbica were filmed by using a close-up, without actually filming the entire area, so it is impossible to conclude where this was actually being filmed. We cannot see any landmarks that would show where the footage was actually being taken. That's my question. And this concludes your cross-examination, and I would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to your first question, my sentence uttered on the tape is, "We are in Izbica, 23rd of June, 1999, 1215 is the time, 15 minutes after noon." This is my opening line when the recording starts, and then I explain what I'm doing. The reason why you don't see subtitles on the screen is that we agreed with the WITNESS organisation for the dates not to appear on the camera itself, but that we mentioned the date. So we deleted the dates from the memory, and I spoke and mentioned the dates. So the subtitle and -- subtitle feature and the memory feature for the date were deactivated. This is the answer to your first question. Your second question has to do with the close-up recording. It is true that the bodies were recorded from close up, and this is because we were not professional cameramen, recorders, and I didn't know how to give instructions to do a proper recording. The idea was to record the bodies and show the world what Serbia committed in Izbica on the 28th of March. So our aim was not to provide the best copy possible because we were not professional; neither was I, neither was he, the doctor. We just wanted to document the event, and in those circumstances we managed to provide a footage that could at least translate to the opinion what happened, that that was Izbica. Then I went with the witnesses on the ground and did some recordings on the ground where they were taken to for execution, and there you can see in more details the valley and the area, which is clearly Izbica. A comparison was made later on, the American intelligence, when they had my tape and when they mentioned it during my briefings, they mentioned that they did an aerial photograph of the area, that they analysed my tape and that they saw the objects on the ground, whether they corresponded with their aerial pictures. And they came to a conclusion that that was Izbica, and then they could openly state to the public that this was Izbica and that this massacre occurred in Izbica and that the recording itself was made in Izbica. During the bombing, during the war, the Serbian Television made a different recording in a different village, presented the Serbs as if Albanians. They spoke Albanian because they knew how to speak Albanian. And they alleged that that place was Izbica, that there was no fighting in Izbica, that nothing had happened there. A long time has passed now, but I think that this material can be found on the internet, and you can see the aim of the Serbian propaganda of the time. They wanted to deny the fact that the massacre happened, and my aim was to show the truth of what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what propaganda you're referring to, Serbian or from Kosovo. That's why I'm --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Television. The Serbian Television made a recording during the bombing campaign. Well, as a matter of fact, before this cassette was issued, I was still in Izbica. At that time I was able to pass on the information about Izbica through the information services of the KLA. I managed to pass this information on that there was a massacre in Izbica and 127 people were executed. This was an information I gave without any photos. I told them that we did have the images, but because of objective reasons it was impossible for them to be given to the public opinion. But in the future, in the near future, we hoped to do that. That near future became true in a month or so when I went to Albania; however, the public opinion was prepared for that. They knew about it. The White House, NATO, the Hague Tribunal, and the media were aware that somebody in Drenice had this tape, and this person will come to Tirana one day and bring it. And fortunately I managed to go to Tirana and take the tape with me. However, while I was in Izbica and I had not passed the tape on, the Serbian Television had recorded something else to say that what is being said about a massacre in Izbica is not true; it's a KLA propaganda, it's Albanian propaganda. However, this was anti-propaganda that wanted to devalue and to say that it was not true that the massacre happened. The fact is that it happened. Serbia had surrounded Kosova so tightly that even the birds could not fly without the Serbs dictating them. That's why they prepared that programme, which, for me, was ridiculous. They took these Serbs, and they spoke on behalf of the Albanians. I think that Serb Television must have those materials now, and you can bring them to the trial, and you can ask them what they did with that. I don't have the material, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As you noticed, Dr. Loshi, I'm not interrupting you, although your answers are always outside the context of the direct questions that I put to you. However, I cannot hold that against you. I just want to ask you or, rather, to remind you about something that has to do with the footage you took in Izbica. We all know full well, and you repeated it to us just now, was to familiarise the public with the crimes of the Serbian police, army, whoever, in relation to the crimes committed in Izbica, as you had put it. My question is the following: Since there is this journalistic rule of who, what, where, why, what should be seen has to be there. What we could see were the corpses. Why was the broader context not there so that we would be sure of the location where this was taken? Because there's not a single house, mountaintop, anything that would clearly show that this was in Izbica. That was my question, and your answer was because you're an amateur. And I'm not going to ask you more about that. I'm going to thank you for your answers, for the answers that you have provided to us, because the truth, no matter what it is deserves an answer. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one thing. I wanted to add one sentence here. You said that the houses cannot be seen here. Well, if you see the graves, that image, you can see the houses and Izbica environment, while where the dead people are lying, that is a meadow, and there are no houses there. And that's why you don't see the houses. However, I will repeat again that we were amateurs, and maybe we should have done it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you've mentioned the cemetery, there were freshly dug graves just before the funeral of these people. Let this really be my last question for today. Who were the people, do you know, who were buried in the graves that can be seen that were actually there before these graves that were dug up subsequently? That can be seen on satellite footage, but I'm asking you about that: Can you tell us - let that be my last question - who were the people who were buried in the graves before these people?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second. I am looking at the question on the monitor. So the question is: Who was buried here before these people? Which people do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before these people, there were other fresh graves there. Can you tell us, who was buried in those fresh graves?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There were no fresh graves there. These were graves that were dug on the 31st of March, most of them. About seven or eight of the graves were opened on the 1st of April. So there was no cemetery there before. This was not a gravesite. [In English] This was not a gravesite. [Interpretation] So this was not a gravesite before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right, all right. Thank you. Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Let me tell you, Your Honours, the Honourable Trial Chamber, that this completes my cross-examination of Mr. Loshi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Kravetz, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you, just a few questions. Could we have Exhibit P291 up on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- Your Honour, may I ask for a very short break, please, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The court officer will assist you, as happened yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the exhibit before you, 291. You were asked some questions by my learned colleague regarding how this was compiled, and you told us that the comments that are included in the comment field in his table we have before us were provided by you. Now, having recently had the opportunity to review this exhibit, are you satisfied that the information contained in the comments field is accurate?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 18 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While that is being brought up, during cross-examination you mentioned that during your previous testimony in the Milutinovic case there had been some confusion regarding the description of two men, and it was suggested to you that these two men were members of the KLA because the description referred to them wearing a military jacket or a military overcoat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on that page. Could we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you able to see those descriptions on this page, Mr. Loshi? I don't know if we have --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It hasn't been zoomed in for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just the English for the witness, if we could zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah, please, the English version. Yeah. "Man, grey/black sweater, military green jacket"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. Are those the entries -- that was one of the entries that was put to you in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the other one: "Man, bluish jacket, military green overcoat, covered in a grey/red woolen blanket." These are the two cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, was the information in those two entries provided by you, or was this provided by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The information was, as I said, that the description was done by the investigator, looking at the pictures on the screen, and then typed in -- typing it down on the paper. So that was done by him, and he was asking if I had a comment in addition to the descriptions. I can't remember. Sometimes I may have helped him in descriptions as well, but I just can't remember it because we were for a few days together. But the comments were mine, and these comments, by the way, were done according to what I saw and according to what I heard when he was playing the tape in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see that next to these two entries there were no comments. Does that mean that you were unable to identify either of these two persons or provide any information in that regard?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not able to identify these people. But if you let me explain, I was a little bit confused about this military green -- military -- any military -- military green jacket and military green coat in these persons, in these two persons, and I was suggesting by the Defence of Milutinovic, and six -- and six -- the trial of six, that these people belonged to KLA. So now I understand that this is just a description of their clothing; it doesn't -- it doesn't mean that these people -- because if you look at these pictures, you can see easily that these people have -- didn't have KLA uniforms, and these were not KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that clarifies the matter. Moving on to a different issue now, you were asked whether the bodies that you filmed at Izbica that appeared in your short video included bodies brought from other places, and you said that the majority of the bodies were found in two big groups and then there was a smaller third group. Now, were these bodies in these two big groups and the smaller group filmed at the location where you found them, you and the others who were participating in this film?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were these the bodies that we saw yesterday when we were viewing the images from your video?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me? Once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were these bodies, the two large groups and the smaller group, the bodies that we saw yesterday when we were --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did any of these three groups include any bodies that were brought by you or by others from other places?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes your questioning in this trial. The Chamber would express its gratitude for your attendance here and the assistance you've given. And you are now, of course, free to return to your normal life and activities. We will now arrange for the court officer to show you out, and thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a pleasure to be able to answer the questions of both parties in this trial, and I hope that I helped the Judges with my answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you ready with your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, we are ready, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before my learned colleague, Mr. Neuner, begins the examination-in-chief, we received the list of exhibits that will probably be admitted into evidence, that will be tendered, but we would first like to look at their 65 ter list. The number is P00023. It's a map of a part of Kosovo. And the routes that the refugees took as they moved in Kosovo have already been drawn into this map. We believe that the witness himself should make those markings, should indicate where the refugees were moving, and not to be merely shown a map with the markings already there, markings indicating where the refugee columns were moving. And this will be and is at issue in this case, and this is why I would like to -- not to admit this exhibit. I am not opposed to the admission of this part of Kosovo, the map of this part of Kosovo, with Orahovac, Prizren, and Djakovica. I don't think it would be proper and it would be, in fact, tantamount to leading the witness, because the witness would then be compelled to confirm and to provide an answer that is already contained in the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have heard what the Defence said, and at this point in time, the document P23 has been put on the list of exhibits eventually to be shown, but this doesn't mean that the exhibit, indeed, will be shown. So I would suggest that my learned friend can put his objection on the record if the Prosecution intends to show the document, which it's not certain at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if you seek to do it, Mr. Neuner, the objection is made, and there is some validity in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will try to elicit answers from the witness that I don't have to use that particular exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or you may need to show him a blank map, if you feel some depiction is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yeah, we have thought about this alternative course of action, and there is 65 ter number 0035 also on this list and there -- this is -- there are some documents -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We leave it to you, Mr. Neuner, to decide what to do about it. Just be aware that there is an objection to your use of this Rule 65 ter exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
